landing.title: Protect your staked SOL
landing.lead: Stakeward puts a lock on the stake accounts you already have. The lock answers to your second key: a wallet from a different seed phrase that only you control. While the lock holds, a thief with your main key, the wallet you stake from, cannot withdraw your stake or make it theirs.

why.title: Why your stake needs a lock
why.body1: Your stake account obeys one key: the key of the wallet you staked from. Whoever gets that key can withdraw the stake, or quietly make it theirs.
why.body2: Keys leak through fake websites, stolen seed phrases, malware, or a hidden step in a transaction you approved. In 2025 and 2026, hundreds of thousands of staked SOL were stolen.
why.body3: Every Solana stake account has a lock built in. Stakeward turns it on for you, with a second key that you hold.

how.title: How it works

step1.title: Lock it with a second key
step1.body: Choose a wallet made from a different seed phrase as your second key. Your main key and your second key approve the lock together, and it is written into your stake accounts on the Solana network. Your stake keeps earning.

step2.title: Get alerts
step2.body: Stakeward checks your stake accounts every few minutes. If you turn on alerts, a Telegram message tells you when anything changes, and before the lock ends.

step3.title: Rescue or withdraw
step3.body: Main key stolen? Before the lock ends, your main key, your second key and a new wallet sign together, and the stake moves to the new wallet, out of the thief's reach. To take your SOL out, your two keys withdraw it together.

how.period: The lock lasts 1, 3, 6 or 12 months. Your second key can extend it before it ends.
how.periodDevnet: On devnet you can also try a 10-minute or 1-hour lock.

protects.title: What Stakeward protects
protects.covered: Native stake: SOL you delegated to a validator from your own wallet. It sits in a stake account that your keys control.

notCovered.lst: Liquid staking tokens (LSTs). They are tokens in your wallet, not stake accounts.
notCovered.exchange: Stake on an exchange. The exchange holds those keys.

needsSecond.withdraw: Withdrawing SOL from the stake account
needsSecond.owner: Handing the stake to another wallet

protects.lockOnlySecond: Only your second key can extend, shorten or remove the lock.
protects.mainAloneTitle: Your main key alone can still

mainAlone.redelegate: Move the stake to another validator
mainAlone.split: Split the stake account into smaller ones, each with the same lock
mainAlone.manager: Change the wallet that manages staking

protects.thief: So while the lock holds, a thief with only your main key can stop your rewards, or move your stake to a validator of their choice. They cannot take the SOL. If an alert surprises you, rescue your stake before the lock ends.

secondKey.title: Your second key: read this first
secondKey.freeze: It cannot take your SOL, but it can keep it locked, even for years.
secondKey.differentSeed: Make it from a different seed phrase. If one seed phrase makes both keys, whoever steals it has both, and the lock stops nothing.
secondKey.apart: Keep it apart from your main key: a hardware wallet, another device, or a person you trust.
secondKey.lost: If you lose it, your SOL is safe but stays locked until the lock's end date. Then your main key alone can withdraw it.
secondKey.stolen: If someone steals it, they cannot take your SOL, but they can keep it locked. Hand the lock to a new second key at once: your recovery card has the command.
secondKey.more: What makes a good second key

cannotDo.title: What Stakeward cannot do
cannotDo.intro: Read this before you protect your stake.

items.scope: It cannot protect liquid staking tokens, stake on an exchange, SOL in your wallet balance or validator vote accounts.
items.mainKeyActions: It cannot stop a thief with your main key from stopping your staking or moving it to another validator. While the lock holds, they still cannot take the SOL.
items.split: It cannot stop a thief with your main key from splitting your stake into many small stake accounts. Each part keeps the lock, but a rescue moves at most {max} of them per run: act early, and extend the lock with your second key first.
items.afterEnd: It cannot keep a thief out after the lock ends. If your main key may be stolen, rescue your stake before that date.
items.lostMain: It cannot help if you lose your main key. Withdrawing always needs the main key, with or without the lock.
items.lostSecond: It cannot shorten the wait if you lose your second key. The lock ends on its date, not before.
items.freeze: It cannot stop whoever holds your second key from keeping your stake locked.
items.sameSeed: It cannot protect you if one seed phrase makes both of your keys.
items.newAccounts: It cannot lock stake accounts you create later in your wallet. Protect each new one too.
items.cliKeys: It cannot make recovery without Stakeward work with keys that live only in a browser: the Solana command line needs your keys on a Ledger or in keypair files.
items.noPower: It cannot move your SOL, sign for you or change your lock. Only your own wallets can.
items.alerts: It cannot promise alerts. If Stakeward is down, alerts come late or not at all. The lock itself keeps working.
items.noKeys: It cannot see your keys or your seed phrase, and it never holds your SOL.

holder.title: You hold a large stake
holder.body: You staked from your own wallet, perhaps with a Ledger, and you want a leaked key not to cost you the stake. Protect it in a few minutes. Your keys stay in your wallets.

team.title: You run a validator or a team treasury
team.body: Lock many stake accounts, one transaction each. Every protected account gets a printable recovery card with Solana command-line steps that work without Stakeward.

secondKeyHolder.title: Someone sent you a link to co-sign
secondKeyHolder.body: Someone made your wallet the second key of their stake. The link shows exactly what their transaction does. Sign only if they asked you by voice or in person. Co-signing costs you nothing and never moves your own SOL.
secondKeyHolder.more: What to check before you co-sign

fees.title: What it costs
fees.intro: Stakeward is free. There is no token and no subscription. You pay only the Solana network fee for each transaction, and Stakeward gets none of it.
fees.perSignature: The network charges {amount} for each signature, plus a tiny fixed priority fee:
fees.extendPayer: Paid by your second key. If it has no SOL, your main key signs too and pays {amount}.
fees.withdrawPayer: Paid by your main key. If the stake is still staking, stopping it first costs {amount}.
fees.depositPayer: A deposit, not a fee: it comes back when you close the account. You need one to sign on another device, and every rescue uses one.
fees.depositUnknown: A small amount set by the network

wallets.title: Which wallets work
wallets.intro: You need two wallets made from different seed phrases. Stakeward talks to browser wallets through the Wallet Standard, such as Phantom, Solflare and Backpack. A Ledger connects through one of them. So far only Phantom has been tested with Stakeward. Solflare, Backpack and Ledger have not been tested yet.
wallets.notVerified: A pair marked Not verified yet has not been tested. Until a pair says Works, try it with a small stake first.

setups.phantom-imported: Phantom, an account imported from another seed phrase

notes.phantom-first: Phantom adds its own safety checks to a transaction, so Phantom signs first.
notes.switch-account: The wallet shares one account at a time. Switch accounts in the wallet between the two signatures.
notes.new-site-warning: The wallet may warn that this site is new. The warning goes away after a few days.
notes.ledger-blind: The Ledger asks for blind signing here. Use another pair with a Ledger.
notes.link-same-browser: Signing by link was tested with both wallets in one browser, not yet from a phone or another computer.

wallets.phone: On a phone, a wallet app's own browser offers only that wallet. There you can check your stake, extend or remove a lock, and co-sign by link. Protect and rescue on a computer.

alerts.title: Alerts in Telegram
alerts.intro: Stakeward checks your protected stake accounts every few minutes. The Stakeward bot sends you a Telegram message when:

events.manager: the wallet that manages staking changes
events.lock: the lock is extended, shortened, removed or handed to another key
events.reminders: the lock ends soon: {days} days before, and when it ends

alerts.turnOn: To turn alerts on, open your accounts and press Get alerts in Telegram. The bot needs only your public wallet address. Send /stop to the bot to turn alerts off.
alerts.anyWallet: Stake data is public, so anyone can follow any wallet. Alerts never contain a key.
alerts.safe: The bot only writes to chats that started it, only links to the Stakeward site and never asks for your seed phrase.
alerts.noGuarantee: Alerts are a free service with no guarantee. If Stakeward is down, alerts come late, but your lock keeps working.

items.chain: The lock lives on the Solana network, inside your stake accounts. It does not depend on Stakeward.
items.browser: Your browser builds every transaction, and your own wallets sign it. Stakeward's server never signs anything and never sees a key.
items.summary: Before each signature you see what the transaction does and what it cannot do. That summary is read from the exact transaction your wallet receives.
items.programs: Transactions use only Solana's own stake program, its system program for signing by link, and fee settings. Stakeward has no program of its own and no token.
items.server: Stakeward's server passes only Stakeward transactions to the network. If it is down, you lose alerts, not SOL. The same server delivers this website, so a hacked server means a hacked website: see the next point.
items.site: If this website were ever hacked, it could ask you to sign something harmful. So read your wallet or Ledger before you approve: wherever it shows the second key or the new wallet, that address must be yours.
items.data: Stakeward keeps only public network data and, if you turn on alerts, your Telegram chat id. No accounts, no logins, no email, no cookies, no analytics.
items.open: The code is open source under the MIT license, with no warranty. Anyone can read it.

recover.title: If Stakeward disappears
recover.body1: Your lock keeps working without Stakeward. It ends on its date, and nothing on Stakeward's side can change it.
recover.body2: If your keys are on a Ledger or in keypair files, the Solana command line can do most of what Stakeward does: withdraw with both keys, move the stake to a new wallet, extend or remove the lock, hand the lock to a new second key. Keys that live only in a browser wallet cannot do this; your main key can withdraw alone once the lock ends.
recover.body3: Every protected stake account has a recovery card with these commands and what to do in each case. Print it and keep it with your keys. It holds no secrets.

devCosign.title: Wallet co-signing test
devCosign.intro: Two wallets sign one transaction that sets a 10-minute lock on a test stake account, by blockhash or durable nonce, in either order. The page shows whether a wallet changed the transaction and how, then sends it and writes a report for the wallet matrix.
devCosign.devnetOnly: Devnet only: test SOL and test accounts. This page is not part of the live site.

sections.walletsIntro: Connect the wallet that owns the test stake as the Main key, and another wallet (or another account of the same wallet) as the Second key.
sections.accountIntro: Stake accounts the Main key can withdraw, read from the network.
sections.runIntro: Builds the transaction, asks each wallet in turn, checks what came back, sends it and reads the account again.
sections.resetIntro: Remove the test lock with the Second key to reuse the same stake account. The 10-minute lock also ends on its own.
sections.reportsIntro: One report per run, kept in this browser. Copy them into the wallet matrix and fill in the last lines.

slots.secondDescription: Becomes the second key of the test lock and co-signs.

setup.title: Set up signing by link
setup.body: Signing on another device needs a small account that keeps the transaction valid until it is signed, even hours later. Your {role} creates it and pays a deposit of {amount}, which comes back when you close it.

setupRescue.title: Set up the link-signing account
setupRescue.body: Rescue always uses a link-signing account: it keeps each transaction valid while three wallets sign, here or on another device. Your {role} creates it and pays a deposit of {amount}, which comes back when you close it.

close.title: Close the link-signing account
close.body: Closing returns {amount} to your {role}. Any link still open stops working.
close.done: Closed. The deposit went back to your {role}.

cosign.intro: Someone asked you to co-sign this transaction. Stakeward reads it only from the link and checks it against the network. Sign only if you expected this request.

stolen.body: Without the second key, the thief cannot withdraw your stake or make it theirs. They can stop the staking and split the stake account. The first lock on this card ends on {date}. After that, the main key alone can withdraw, so the thief can too. Move every stake account to a new wallet well before then, at least a day earlier.
stolen.time: If you cannot finish soon, first extend the lock with the second key alone, as in “The lock is about to end”. The thief cannot undo that, and the stolen key signs nothing.
stolen.cleanDevice: Work on a computer you trust, not the one where the main key may have leaked. If you can, keep the second key and the new wallet each on its own Ledger, made from its own seed phrase: a Ledger key never leaves the device.
stolen.newWallet: Create a new wallet from a new seed phrase and send it about {amount}: it pays the fees. For the command line use a new Ledger, a spare Ledger reset with a new seed phrase, or a keypair file made with solana-keygen new on that trusted computer. Never use the Ledger that holds your main key or your second key, not even another account on it: every account on one Ledger comes from its seed phrase. Do not send SOL to the stolen main key: a bot may take it at once.

When every stake account is moved, run the command that lists them again: the thief may have split off another one in the meantime. Move each one it still lists, until it lists none. From then on the new wallet is your main key: use it wherever this card says <MAIN_KEY>. Then open this card again at the address at the bottom and print it. Keep this copy as well: only this one can list the stolen key's stake accounts.
stolen.restake: If the stake stopped earning, stake it again from the new wallet: in Stakeward, or in a wallet app that holds the new wallet.

stolenSecond.body: The thief cannot take your SOL, but they can move the lock date or hand the lock to their own key, and freeze the stake. Act first: hand the lock to a new second key. groups.keys: Your keys, and what can go wrong

what.a:
A free website that turns on the lock built into your Solana stake accounts. While the lock holds, withdrawing your SOL or handing the stake to another wallet needs your second key to sign too: a wallet of yours made from a different seed phrase.

Stakeward is not a wallet. It does not hold your SOL, and it has no program or token of its own.

custody.q: Does Stakeward hold my SOL or my keys?
custody.a: No. Your SOL stays in your own stake accounts, and your keys stay in your own wallets. Stakeward never asks for your seed phrase. If anyone asks for it in Stakeward's name, it is a scam.

rewards.a: Yes. The lock does not touch staking. Your stake stays with its validator and keeps earning rewards.

wallet-app.q: Can I still use my wallet's staking screen?
wallet-app.a:
Yes, to stake, to unstake and to change validators. Withdrawing there fails while the lock holds: withdraw through Stakeward with both keys, or wait until the lock ends.

A new stake account you create there starts without a lock: protect it too. Merging a locked stake account with one that has a different lock fails.

lock-ends.q: What happens when the lock ends?
lock-ends.a:
It ends at 00:00 UTC on its end date. From then on your main key alone controls the stake again, as before.

The lock does not renew itself. If you turned on alerts, Stakeward reminds you {days} days before. Your second key can extend the lock any time before it ends. After it ends, protect the stake again in Stakeward.

period.q: Which lock period should I choose?
period.a: Six months suits most people. A shorter lock means a shorter wait if you lose your second key. A longer lock means fewer renewals. Your second key can extend it before it ends.

thefts.q: Has staked SOL really been stolen like this?
thefts.a:
Yes. In September 2025, about 192,600 SOL left SwissBorg's staking: a hacked staking partner hid a change of the withdrawal key inside a routine unstaking transaction, and SwissBorg's own signers approved it. With a lock on, such a change fails unless the second key signs too.

In January 2026, 261,854 staked SOL were unstaked and taken from Step Finance after attackers got into its executives' devices.

good-second-key.q: What makes a good second key?
good-second-key.a:
A wallet made from a different seed phrase than your main key. A hardware wallet, such as a Ledger, or a wallet on another device is best. Stakeward has not been tested with a Ledger, so try one with a small stake first. Keep its seed phrase apart from your main key's.

A second account in the same wallet app usually comes from the same seed phrase. Then it does not protect you, unless you imported that account from its own seed phrase.

Use your second key only to co-sign Stakeward transactions; do not connect it to other sites. One signature on a fake site can hand your lock to a thief's key.

different-seed.q: Why must the two keys come from different seed phrases?
different-seed.a: One seed phrase makes all of its wallets. If one phrase makes both keys, whoever steals it has both, and the lock stops nothing. Stakeward asks you to confirm this, but it cannot check it for you.

someone-else.q: Can another person hold my second key?
someone-else.a: Yes, for example a family member or a colleague with their own wallet. They co-sign by link from their own device. They can never move your SOL, but they can keep it locked by moving the lock date. Choose someone you would trust with that.

main-stolen.q: My main key was stolen. What now?
main-stolen.a:
Stay calm: while the lock holds, the thief cannot take the stake. They may still stop your staking or move it to another validator. They may also split it into many small stake accounts. Each part keeps the lock.

Rescue before the lock ends: after that time the thief can withdraw. One rescue run moves at most {rescueMax} stake accounts, and Stakeward cannot move them all at once. If you need more time, or there are many, first extend the lock on each with your second key alone, then rescue them run by run.

On a device you trust, make a new wallet with a new seed phrase and put about {rescueAmount} on it. Then open Rescue: your main key, your second key and the new wallet sign together, and the stake moves to the new wallet. Afterwards, stake it again from the new wallet.

Do not send SOL to the stolen wallet: thieves' bots empty it within seconds.

main-lost.q: I lost my main key. Can Stakeward help?
main-lost.a:
No. Withdrawing or moving a stake always needs its main key, with or without the lock. Keep a safe backup of your main key's seed phrase.

If someone else may have your lost main key, extend the lock with your second key before each end date. The stake stays stuck, but nobody can take it.

second-lost.q: I lost my second key. What now?
second-lost.a: Your SOL is safe, but it stays locked until the lock's end date. Then your main key alone can withdraw it, or protect it again with a new second key. Nobody can shorten the wait, not even Stakeward.

second-stolen.q: My second key was stolen. What now?
second-stolen.a:
The thief cannot take your SOL. They can move the lock date far ahead, or hand the lock to another key.

If you still have the second key, hand the lock to a new second key at once. Your recovery card has the one command for it; it needs the Solana command line. In Stakeward today: remove the lock with the old second key, then protect the stake again with a new one right away. In between, your main key alone controls the stake.

If the thief changed the lock first, your SOL is still yours, but it stays locked until the date they set.

both-stolen.q: What if both keys are stolen?
both-stolen.a: Then the thief can take the stake. That is why the two keys must come from different seed phrases and be kept apart.

change-second-key.q: Can I change my second key?
change-second-key.a: Not in Stakeward yet. The Solana command line does it in one step: see your recovery card. In Stakeward, remove the lock with your old second key, then protect the stake again with the new one right away. In between, your main key alone controls the stake.

locked-by-other.q: Why does my stake account say Locked by a second key?
locked-by-other.a:
Its lock is held by a key that this browser does not know as yours. On a new device or in another browser, your own lock looks like this until you connect your second key on your accounts page; then it says Protected or Expiring soon. Stakeward never calls a lock Protected before that: the network does not say whose key it is.

Once this browser knows your second key, a lock held by any other key says Locked by another key instead. If you never set such a lock, someone else holds it, and only they can change it. They still cannot withdraw your SOL without your main key.

fake-site.q: How do I avoid a fake Stakeward site?
fake-site.a:
Type the address yourself or use a bookmark, and do not follow links from strangers. A fake site could try to make a thief's wallet your second key. On a Ledger, check the address shown as New authority: it must be your second key. That name comes from the source code of Ledger's Solana app, not from a test on a device. Browser wallets may not show it.

Afterwards, open your accounts from your bookmark with your second key connected. Each stake account you protected must say Protected or Expiring soon. One that says Locked by another key is not locked by the key you connected. If you did not set that lock, its holder can keep the stake locked, but cannot withdraw it without your main key.

check-explorer.q: How can I check my lock without Stakeward?
check-explorer.a: Stakeward reads the network through its own server, so a hacked server could show you a wrong state. To check without it, open Solana Explorer by typing explorer.solana.com yourself, and look up your stake account. At the top it must say "Account is locked! Lockup expires on" and the date you chose. If that line is missing, your stake account is not locked. Under Authorities, the Lockup Authority Address must be your second key and the Withdraw Authority Address must be your main key.

ledger.a: Stakeward builds every transaction in the shape the Ledger Solana app can show as readable fields. The list below comes from that app's source code. This is what each one should show:

wallet-warning.q: Why does my wallet show a warning?
wallet-warning.a: Wallets warn about sites they have not reviewed yet, and about transactions that need more than one signature. Protecting, withdrawing and rescuing always need two or three signatures. Read the warning, then check the addresses your wallet shows. Never approve if the second key or the new wallet shown is not yours.

co-sign.q: Someone sent me a link to co-sign. Is it safe?
co-sign.a:
The link holds a transaction, never a key. The page reads it only from the link, checks it against the network and shows what it does.

Sign only if the owner asked you by voice or in person. For a withdrawal or a rescue, check the address with them the same way. A thief with the owner's main key would send exactly such a link.

Co-signing costs you nothing and never moves your own SOL.

phone.q: Can I use Stakeward on my phone?
phone.a: Partly. A phone wallet's own browser offers only that one wallet. There you can check your stake, extend or remove a lock, and co-sign by link. Protecting and rescuing need two or three wallets at once, so do them on a computer.

many-accounts.q: Can I protect many stake accounts at once?
many-accounts.a: Yes. Each stake account gets its own transaction. If your wallet can, it approves them all in one request. If only some go through, Stakeward shows which ones are protected and lets you try again for the rest.

staking-service.q: A staking service manages my stake. Can I lock it?
staking-service.a: Be careful. Some services, for example Marinade Native, manage your stake account for you. With a lock on, the service may not be able to merge or rebalance it. Ask the service first. Stakeward marks such accounts on your accounts page.

free.a: Yes. You pay only Solana network fees, and Stakeward gets none of them. There is no token, and Stakeward takes no payment in crypto. Protection, alerts, withdrawing and rescue stay free.

deposit.a: Signing on another device needs a small helper account that keeps the transaction valid until the other device signs, even hours later. The network asks for {deposit} to keep it open, and your wallet gets it back when you close the account. Every rescue uses one.

privacy.q: What does Stakeward know about me?
privacy.a:
Only public data. Stakeward's server keeps the public state of the stake accounts it watches and, if you turn on alerts, your Telegram chat id. There are no accounts, logins, email, cookies or analytics.

Your browser remembers which wallet you used for each key and which stake accounts you protected, so it can warn you when a lock ends. That stays on your device.

stop-alerts.a: Send /stop to the Stakeward bot in Telegram. It stops all alerts for that chat and forgets the chat.

on-chain.q: What exactly does Stakeward change on the network?
on-chain.a:
It sends one SetLockupChecked instruction per stake account. The lockup's unix_timestamp becomes the end date at 00:00 UTC, its epoch is left unchanged, and the custodian becomes your second key. The withdrawer signs, and so does the new custodian.

While the lockup is in force, the stake program needs the custodian's signature for Withdraw and for Authorize(Withdrawer). Deactivate, DelegateStake, Split and Authorize(Staker) still need only the staker.

existing-accounts.q: Isn't a lockup set only when a stake account is created?
existing-accounts.a: The documentation says so. The stake program's code (Meta::set_lockup) lets the withdrawer set a new lockup on an existing account whenever no lockup is in force. While one is in force, only the custodian can change it. Stakeward's checks of this against the real stake program are in the repository.

terms.q: What do custodian, withdrawer and staker mean?
terms.a:
They are the stake program's own names, which your Ledger and the Solana command line use.

Main key: the withdraw authority, or withdrawer. Usually it is also the stake authority, or staker.

Stake authority (staker): the key that manages staking, that is delegating, stopping and splitting. A staking service may hold it.

Second key: the lockup custodian.

New wallet: the key a rescue makes both the withdraw authority and the stake authority.

cli.q: Can I do all of this with the Solana CLI?
cli.a:
Mostly. Each recovery card lists the solana commands for its stake accounts: withdraw-stake and stake-authorize-checked with --custodian, and stake-set-lockup to extend or remove a lock. They need your keys as keypair files or on a Ledger, all on one computer; they do not need Stakeward.

One gap: Solana CLI {version} refuses to set a new lock after the old one ended, so protect again in Stakeward.

programs.q: Which programs do the transactions use?
programs.a: Only the stake program, the system program (to create, advance and close a durable nonce account for signing by link) and Compute Budget, with a fixed limit and price. There are no address lookup tables, and each transaction touches one stake account. Phantom may append Lighthouse assertion instructions at the end. Stakeward accepts only that, and checks that nothing else changed.

audit.a: No. There is no Stakeward program on the network to audit: the lock is the stake program's own feature. The website's code is open, and every kind of transaction is tested against the real stake program. Read the code before you trust it with a large stake, or ask someone you trust to read it.
